title: Introducing Lumma-Fev-v2
gist: FrontiersMind released Lumma-Fev-4B-v2 and 27B-v2, open Apache-2.0 decision models that return option probabilities in one forward pass with no text generation. They report 87.3% (27B) and 82.4% (4B) average accuracy over eight public benchmarks versus 81.2% for TypeSafe Jev 1.13.0, plus better calibration; Jev still leads on BBH and JudgeBench.

insights.claim: Lumma-Fev-v2 models take a state and typed questions and return a probability for every option in a single forward pass without generating text, so there is nothing to parse.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Probability-returning classifiers replace brittle text parsing in automation pipelines, enabling thresholds and human-review routing.
insights.quote: It never generates text, so there is nothing to parse.

insights.claim: The v2 family spans 0.1B to 27B on one interface, built on the authors' own Nandi-Mini-150M and Lumma-0.6B-Base for small sizes and on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.8-27B for larger ones, so users can scale without changing code.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Shared interface across sizes lowers switching costs and lets buyers trade cost against accuracy.

insights.claim: The 27B-v2 uses bidirectional attention in its full-attention layers (Gated DeltaNet layers stay causal), trains on about 300K samples versus about 100K for v1, and was trained with the open-source decisionformer library.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Encoder-style attention suits decision tasks where the whole prompt is known before scoring; more data is the other lever.

insights.claim: Lumma-Fev-27B-v2 averages 87.3% across eight public benchmarks and the 4B averages 82.4%, versus 81.2% for TypeSafe Jev 1.13.0.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: An open 4B model beating a hosted incumbent on average undermines the pricing power of closed decision-model services, though the benchmarks are vendor-selected.

insights.claim: Jev still leads on reasoning-heavy benchmarks, scoring 91.1 on BBH versus 83.9 for the 27B and 80.6 on JudgeBench versus 77.4, which the authors call the family's main remaining gap.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Honest disclosure that reasoning-heavy decisions still favor Jev; buyers with such workloads should test before switching.
insights.quote: reasoning remains the main gap for the family

insights.claim: The 0.1B model scores 93.2% on Emotion, the top result in the chart, and beats Jev on AG News and BANKING77, but averages only 60.4% because it collapses on reading-heavy tasks such as BBH (35.9) and RAGTruth (37.7).
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Tiny models are viable for simple classification at very low cost but not for reasoning-dependent decisions.

insights.claim: On an internal 400-row multilingual set, the 27B averages 87.7% across Hindi, Tamil and Kannada versus 79.7% for Jev, with the 4B at 85.3%.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Indic-language strength is a differentiator for Indian enterprise automation; benchmark is internal and translated by Claude, so treat as indicative.

insights.claim: Both v2 models beat Jev on log loss, ECE and Brier, and pooled over 11,657 rows ECE is 0.004 for the 4B and 0.010 for the 27B versus 0.091 for Jev.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Calibrated confidence is what makes automated routing safe, so this is the product's key selling point beyond accuracy.

insights.claim: Jev is overconfident: when it states 90% confidence it is right about 80% of the time.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Overconfidence in the incumbent undermines threshold-based automation built on its scores.
insights.quote: when Jev says 90%, it is right about 80% of the time

insights.claim: On the Indic benchmark the 27B's ECE of 0.084 is close to but slightly worse than Jev's 0.080, and the 4B's ECE of 0.096 is higher than Jev's, so calibration advantage is not universal.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Users in Indic-language settings should fit thresholds on their own data.
insights.quote: fit your thresholds on your own labeled traffic

insights.claim: The 27B-v2 needs about 55 GB of free GPU memory (a single 80 GB card), BF16 weights, 8,192 tokens of context, and lumma-fev 0.3 or later, with Apache 2.0 licensing and a TypeSafe-compatible HTTP API.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: A TypeSafe-compatible endpoint and permissive license make drop-in migration from the hosted incumbent straightforward.

insights.claim: Score-type questions are accepted but untested because the models were trained only on yes/no (noul) and choice questions.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Capability boundary to check before relying on numeric scoring.

insights.claim: The 0.1B-v2 and 0.6B-v2 models are announced as coming soon, so the full 0.1B to 27B family is not yet released.
insights.speaker: Rohit
insights.so_what: Small-model releases extend the cost curve downward for edge or high-volume classification.
